scenes.text: Seven mornings, from fifteen hundred to twenty one hundred. In each one, you wake up as a different kid, on a school day. Or a day with no school at all. You start out learning a trade with your hands. You end up somewhere your tutor might not even be human. And at the end, you'll find out what the word school really means.

scenes.text: You wake up in fifteen hundred, in London. It's still dark. Next door, a hammer's already going, and the street smells of wet straw and wood smoke. Did you know that historians estimate only about one woman in a hundred in England could even write her own name? So what is school to you? Something for other people. For priests, and rich boys. Most children learn by working. If you're a craftsman's son, you're apprenticed. Usually seven years, living in your master's house, learning his trade by doing it. If you're lucky enough for grammar school, lessons often start at six in the morning. In Latin. And if you're a prince? Nine year old Prince Henry, the future Henry the Eighth, has a teacher all to himself, the poet John Skelton. One teacher. One child. Remember that. In fifteen twenty four, a rebel preacher, Martin Luther, writes to the leaders of German cities. Build schools, he says. For boys, and for girls. Partly so everyone can read the Bible. Why would a whole town care if a farmer's daughter can read? Soon, a colony across the ocean will write it into law.

scenes.text: You wake up in sixteen forty seven, in a farming town in Massachusetts. There's frost on the window, and the cows need milking before breakfast. Did you know that one of America's first school laws begins by blaming the devil? It says it's a chief project of that old deluder, Satan, to keep men from the knowledge of the Scriptures. So what's school to you now? A way to read God's word, with your own eyes. Five years earlier, a law told parents and masters to teach their children to read. Lots of them didn't bother. So now, any town with fifty households has to hire someone to teach reading and writing. A hundred households? A grammar school too, or the town pays a fine. You learn your letters between the chores, and on Sunday, you hear why they matter. All over Protestant Europe, churches want people reading. But a church can only ask. In the next century, a king will order it. And he'll ban one thing every kid on Earth looks forward to.

scenes.text: You wake up in seventeen sixty three, in a village in Prussia. It's autumn. The war's just over, the harvest's in, and the pastor has news from the king. Did you know that Frederick the Great's new school law banned school holidays? Not even at harvest time. So what is school now? An order. From the king. Every boy and girl, from the age of five until about thirteen. Skip it, and your parents can be fined. In winter, you're in class from eight to eleven, and one to four. In summer, just a few hours, because there are cows to herd. The law even says, hire a shepherd, so the children can go to school. Your teacher might be an old soldier. Many early village teachers were. You might have heard school was invented to make obedient factory workers. Historians say it's not that simple. Prussia was still a land of farms. The king and his church wanted loyal, God fearing, disciplined subjects. And plenty of families just ignored the rules. But one teacher per village is slow, and expensive. In London, a young man thinks he can teach the poor for almost nothing. His trick? Make the children the teachers.

scenes.text: You wake up in eighteen ten, in London, on Borough Road. You walk into one enormous hall. Hundreds of children, in long rows. And just one master. Did you know that this school's founder, Joseph Lancaster, claimed one master could run a school of more than a thousand children? Older kids teach the younger ones, in small groups. You write your letters in sand, with your finger, because paper costs money. Misbehave, and you might be hoisted above the classroom, in a cage. Really. Lancaster thought it beat the cane. So what's school to you? A machine. For teaching the poor, by the hundred, as cheaply as possible. By the time Lancaster dies, more than twelve hundred schools are said to use his system. Then the law steps in. In eighteen eighty, school becomes compulsory in England, from five to ten. In eighteen ninety one, for most families, it becomes free. Now every child has to go. But in the next century, school stops being something you're forced into. It turns into something people fight for.

scenes.text: You wake up in nineteen forty eight, in a small American town. It's June. Graduation day. Your mum's ironing your gown, and the radio's on. Did you know that in nineteen ten, fewer than one in five American teenagers went to high school? By nineteen forty, it was about seven in ten. Your grandad probably left school young, to work. You're staying to the end, because a diploma opens doors. So what is school to you now? A ladder. Every year you climb gets you closer to a better job. And that December, in Paris, the United Nations writes it down for the whole world. Everyone has the right to education. Free, at least in the early years. So now school is a right. And a ladder. And a building you walk to every morning. But about seventy years later, most of the world's schools would close. Almost at once.

In nineteen eighty four, an American researcher, Benjamin Bloom, reported that tutored students did better than ninety eight percent of students taught in a normal class. Then, in twenty twenty four, a World Bank pilot in Nigeria gave students an AI tutor, twice a week, with their teachers guiding them.
